title: Chemical pressure and vacancies in crystals under nonhydrostatic stress
abstract: Inhomogeneous stress is a driving force for diffusion of vacancies in crystals. The other way around a non-uniform distribution of vacancies induces stress. The accepted theory of composition-stress coupling in crystals is Larché-Cahn (LC) theory. Composition is defined in terms of the population of lattice sites with a limit of one-particle per site. Coupling is modelled by adding a compositional strain term to the elastic strain in the constitutive relation for stress. An alternative mechanism, proposed here, is letting the site binding energy vary with spatial (deformed) density. This generates a chemical pressure adding to the elastic stress. The governing equations for this model are derived using non-equilibrium continuum thermodynamic methods. The gradient of the chemical pressure has a dual function acting both as the drift force for migration and as an effective internal one body force in the Cauchy equation for the elastic stress. The practical evaluation presented in the paper is restricted to equilibrium properties. We examine the effect of externally applied non-hydrostatic stress, either in the form of surface tractions or a one-body force density (gravitation). The model system is a one component crystal with a fixed number of lattice sites. The number of particles can be variable but is always smaller than the number of lattice sites. The linear elastic response is modelled by the standard Lamé stress tensor. The results for systems deformed by surface tractions are in qualitative agreement with LC theory allowing for differences in the expression for the elastic moduli. Deviations are more serious for the crystal deformed by gravitation.
summary: This work develops a thermodynamic model for crystalline solids that accounts for the coupling between mechanical stress and the concentration of vacancies via a chemically induced pressure. By deriving governing equations from non-equilibrium thermodynamics, the authors propose an alternative to standard theories, showing how chemical potential gradients act as internal body forces under external stress.
main_problem: The paper investigates the coupling between mechanical stress and chemical equilibrium (composition/vacancy concentration) in crystalline solids under nonhydrostatic stress.
main_result: The proposed chemical pressure model generates an internal density-dependent stress that modifies the standard Larché-Cahn (LC) thermomechanical response, showing qualitative agreement with LC theory for surface tractions.
method: The theory is derived using non-equilibrium continuum thermodynamic methods, formulating governing equations based on free energy density and chemical potential gradients.
model_or_system: The system is a one-component crystal with a fixed number of lattice sites, modeled as a compressible lattice gas. The coupling mechanism is based on letting the site binding energy vary with spatial density, generating a chemical pressure.
key_observables: Chemical pressure, vacancy number ($N_v$), stress tensor (Cauchy/Piola), and chemical potential ($\mu$).
important_parameters: Nonhydrostatic stress (surface tractions, gravitation), temperature ($T$), and lattice site density ($s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to equilibrium properties, and the model assumes a single-component crystal with no interstitial atoms.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first defining the free energy density incorporating elastic and binding energy terms. It then derives coupled balance equations for force and chemical potential, showing how the chemical pressure gradient acts as both a drift force and an internal body force.
why_interesting: While focused on classical condensed matter, the rigorous application of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and the coupling of multiple degrees of freedom (mechanical strain and chemical composition) mirrors complex open quantum systems where energy and particle exchange are coupled.
